name: What is the best shower option for accessible bathroom remodeling?

mainEntity.name: Is a curbless shower better than a walk-in shower, and when does each make sense for accessibility?
mainEntity.text: Is a curbless shower better than a walk-in shower, and when does each make sense for accessibility?

acceptedAnswer.text: For accessibility, a curbless shower is typically the strongest choice because it eliminates the curb that creates a tripping or transfer barrier. It also supports wheelchair users, people with walkers, and anyone planning for aging in place. A walk-in shower with a low threshold can still be practical in some remodels, especially when waterproofing or slab conditions make a fully curbless build harder to execute. The best option depends on the floor structure, drain location, and whether the bathroom can be recessed enough to create proper slope. In luxury remodels, curbless showers can be paired with bench seating, handheld sprayers, and slip-resistant tile. The main risk is poor drainage if the shower is not engineered correctly, which can lead to standing water. A knowledgeable contractor should confirm framing depth, waterproofing details, and code-compliant slope before approving the design.
acceptedAnswer.description: A curbless shower is usually the most accessible option because it removes the step-over barrier and allows easier wheelchair or walker access. A walk-in shower with a low threshold can still work when drainage, slope, and entry width are designed correctly, but it is less seamless than a true zero-threshold shower.
